texto: ## 9. Blocking language

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: Describe physical movement with six inputs.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: - Who moves.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: - Where they start.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: - Where they end.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: - What object they touch.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: - What they look at.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: - What their body reveals emotionally.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: Example.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto:
```text
The man stands in the kitchen doorway, shoulders collapsed. He slowly approaches the refrigerator, opens it with hesitation, leans into the cold light, then freezes when he sees the empty shelves.
```

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 9. Blocking language
texto: This beats "a sad man goes to the fridge" because it is playable by the model frame by frame.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 10. Translating uncommon terms
texto: ## 10. Translating uncommon terms

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 10. Translating uncommon terms
texto: Common terms (section 2) work by name. For rarer cinematography terms, keep the term **and** translate it into observable change, or the model guesses:

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 10. Translating uncommon terms
texto:
```text
Term + target subject + visual change + foreground/background relationship + direction or speed
```

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 10. Translating uncommon terms
texto: Example.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 10. Translating uncommon terms
texto:
```text
Rack focus: shift focus smoothly from the leaves in the foreground to the person
in the background. The leaves gradually blur while the person's face changes
from soft to sharp.
```

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 10. Translating uncommon terms
texto: Same pattern for snorricam, contra-zoom variants, tilt-shift, split diopter, speed ramps with specific curves. Numeric aperture and focal-length values are allowed, but the intended visible result phrased in words is what actually steers the model.

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: ## 11. Transition vocabulary

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: Named transitions every current model understands to some degree (Seedance 2.5 honors them explicitly — templates in `seedance-25.md` §10):

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **natural cut** — plain edit point, model picks the framing change

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **fade in / fade out** — to or from black

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **dissolve** — cross-fade, 1-2 seconds of overlap

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **white flash / black flash** — one-frame blast, impact punctuation

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **wipe** — new frame pushes the old one off

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **occlusion mask** — a foreground object covers the lens, the new scene is revealed behind it

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **match cut** — similar shape or motion bridges two scenes (moon → latte)

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **action cut / whip pan** — cut hidden inside fast motion with motion blur

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **motion relay** — subject exits frame A mid-move and lands in frame B continuing it

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **zoom-through** — camera dives through a pupil, keyhole or window into the next scene

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: - **ink-wash dissolve** — stylized bleed, common in guofeng / animation work

encabezado: Camera, lighting, color, sound vocabulary › 11. Transition vocabulary
texto: Rules of use. Name the transition and the exact moment it fires. One transition type per cut. When the choice is open, delegate: "choose the most suitable from [natural cut / occlusion mask / match cut] for the style of this film."

Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: ## 1. Core law. Scene formula

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: A scene exists only when all five elements are present.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto:
```text
Scene = hero's desire + obstacle + space geometry + controlled gaze + editing rhythm
```

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: If any element is missing, the scene collapses into decoration.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: - Desire. What does the character want right now in this specific second.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: - Obstacle. What blocks them. Object, person, fear, distance, rule.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: - Space geometry. Who stands where. Who has the power position. Which direction is threat, which is escape.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: - Controlled gaze. Where the viewer's eye is forced to look, one focal point per frame.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: - Editing rhythm. How long each shot lives, where the pause lands, where the cut bites.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 1. Core law. Scene formula
texto: Before writing a prompt, name each of these in one sentence. If you cannot, the scene is not ready.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt.
texto: ## 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt.
texto: The scene formula tells you **what a scene is**. The Details Law tells you **how every shot must be written**. Skip it and even a perfect dramaturgical structure produces mush on screen.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt.
texto: > Every shot owns three concrete physical details: one environmental pressure, one physical micro-action, one sound or visual motif anchor.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › The three-detail rule
texto: ### The three-detail rule

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › The three-detail rule
texto: For each shot in the storyboard or prompt, before it is sent, the writer commits to:

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › The three-detail rule
texto: 1. **Environmental pressure.** A physical fact about the space that carries the emotion. Cold refrigerator light. Wet asphalt. Flickering ceiling tube. Steam from the kettle. Rain on one specific windowpane. A buzzing AC unit. Tight corridor walls. Mirror reflection. (See §9 — Environment plays.)

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › The three-detail rule
texto: 2. **Physical micro-action on the body.** The emotion translated into the actor's body. Jaw locks. Knuckles whiten. Lips press flat. Eyes drop a quarter-inch. He swallows hard. Fingers curl against the doorframe. The actor's body is the only place where feelings render — names of feelings do not.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › The three-detail rule
texto: 3. **Sound anchor or visual motif.** A recurring perceptual hook tied to the spine of the piece. Stomach growl repeated three times. Reflection in dark glass on every transition. The same musical sting at every Crack beat. The clock's second hand. Footsteps in an empty corridor.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › The three-detail rule
texto: A shot with zero of these is filler. A shot with one is thin. Strong shots carry all three. The writer's job is to do this work — the model cannot infer it.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › What is banned
texto: ### What is banned

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › What is banned
texto: Words that mark a writer being lazy. Each one is a placeholder for absent detail.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › What is banned
texto: - "cinematic", "professional", "high quality", "masterpiece", "stunning", "epic", "amazing"

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › What is banned
texto: - "beautiful lighting", "dynamic camera", "intense moment", "powerful scene"

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › What is banned
texto: - "he is sad", "she is angry", "he is afraid" — emotions named without a body

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › What is banned
texto: Replace each with concrete physical facts. If a writer cannot do that, the scene is not yet thought through.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › How details map to dramaturgy
texto: ### How details map to dramaturgy

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › How details map to dramaturgy
texto: Each layer of dramaturgy has a default detail register:

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › How details map to dramaturgy
texto: - Scene formula → environmental pressure (the geometry and atmosphere of the obstacle).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › How details map to dramaturgy
texto: - Three-jobs rule → physical micro-action (the body shifts when emotion / action / pressure shifts).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › How details map to dramaturgy
texto: - Five anchors → sound and visual motif (the motif is the anchor, the final image carries the motif).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 2. Second law. Details intensify emotion. Laziness kills the prompt. › How details map to dramaturgy
texto: If a shot's detail set does not match its dramaturgical function, the function will not land on screen.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 3. The three-jobs rule
texto: ## 3. The three-jobs rule

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 3. The three-jobs rule
texto: Every shot must do at least one of three things. If it does none, delete it.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 3. The three-jobs rule
texto: - Change emotion (in hero, viewer, or the dynamic between characters).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 3. The three-jobs rule
texto: - Advance action (new physical event, new information, new position).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 3. The three-jobs rule
texto: - Increase pressure (stakes rise, clock ticks, space tightens, witness appears).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 3. The three-jobs rule
texto: "Beautiful establishing shot" is not a job. "Beautiful hero shot of product" is not a job. Either the frame works for one of these three, or it is a fantik (wrapper without candy).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: ## 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: From the editor of Apocalypse Now, The Godfather Part II, and The English Patient. The priority order when deciding where to cut. Each item is weighted heavier than the sum of everything below it.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: 1. **Emotion (51%).** Does the cut honor the emotional truth of the moment. What does the viewer feel now vs. what they should feel next.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: 2. **Story (23%).** Does the cut advance story or reveal character.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: 3. **Rhythm (10%).** Does the cut fall on a musical beat of the scene.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: 4. **Eye-trace (7%).** Where is the viewer's gaze at the moment of the cut. Does the new shot receive that gaze naturally.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: 5. **2D plane (5%).** Does the cut respect the axis of screen direction.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: 6. **3D space (4%).** Does the cut respect the geometry of the real location.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 4. Walter Murch Rule of Six
texto: Practical consequence. Cutting for "динамика" (pace for its own sake) sits at item 3. If you cut there without serving items 1 and 2, the result is TikTok-ad for the attention-deficit.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: ## 5. Blocking as choreography of desire

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: Blocking is not "where the actor stands." Blocking is a visual answer to "what does the character want and from whom."

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: For every character in the scene, name.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: - What they want now.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: - Who or what they move toward.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: - Who or what they move away from.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: - Whom they corner.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: - To whom they yield space.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto: - What gesture reveals the hidden desire.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 5. Blocking as choreography of desire
texto:
Bad. "He stands near the window."
Good. "He edges toward the window but his shoulder stays angled back toward her, as if the conversation still holds him."

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: ## 6. Staging controls subtext

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: Staging is the arrangement of people, objects, and camera inside the frame. Before dialogue, staging already tells the conflict.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: Power signals in staging.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: - The standing character dominates the seated one.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: - The character in the doorway controls the room.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: - The character behind glass or in reflection is psychologically distant.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: - The character in shadow carries threat or grief.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: - Negative space around a character signals isolation.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: - Tight framing signals suffocation.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: - Shared frame without eye contact signals broken intimacy.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: Spielberg, Kubrick, Iñárritu often build entire scenes where the staging states the conflict before a line is spoken.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 6. Staging controls subtext
texto: Before writing a prompt, name the power dynamic the staging reveals.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: ## 7. Camera must have a reason

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: Fincher rule. Every camera movement answers "what changed?" If the answer is nothing, the camera is static.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: Reasons for camera movement.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: - A character made a decision and the camera follows the shift.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: - New information arrived in the frame.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: - Pressure escalated and the camera tightens.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: - The character looked, and the camera reveals what they saw.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: - A gesture pulled focus, and the camera rack-focused.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto: - The space changed (door opened, someone entered).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 7. Camera must have a reason
texto:
Bad. "Cinematic gliding camera movement."
Good. "Push-in starts on 'I don't know' and stops on her jaw locking."

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria
texto: ## 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria
texto: Spielberg principle. Even in chaos, the viewer must know.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria
texto: - Where the hero is.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria
texto: - Where the threat is.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria
texto: - Which direction is escape.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria
texto: - Which direction is decision.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria
texto: High craft means fast, nervous, and still readable. Random whip-pans and strobe cuts without geography destroy drama. The fastest action scenes in cinema (Spielberg, Miller, early Bay) are built on a clear geometric map maintained through every cut.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 8. Spatial clarity beats montage hysteria
texto: Before writing a fast-cut sequence, sketch the geography in one sentence. "Hero moves left-to-right. Threat enters from the top of the frame. Exit is off-camera right."

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: ## 9. Environment plays

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: Kurosawa principle. Weather and environment are characters. They amplify state.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: Translate this to a short video by leaning on one environmental pressure.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: - Flickering fluorescent light signals decay, bureaucracy, dread.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: - Rain on a window signals grief withheld.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: - Steam from a kettle signals suppressed anger.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: - A buzzing air conditioner signals dissociation.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: - Wet asphalt at night signals guilt.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: - A tight corridor signals the walls closing in.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: - A mirror or glass surface signals self-reckoning.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: - Overhead cold office light signals judgment.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 9. Environment plays
texto: Pick one environmental pressure per scene and let it carry the emotion.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method
texto: ## 10. Three-layer storyboard method

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method
texto: Build storyboards in three layers, in this order. Skipping a layer produces pretty but empty output.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 1. Dramatic beats
texto: ### Layer 1. Dramatic beats

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 1. Dramatic beats
texto: For a 60-90 second piece, a reliable beat map.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 1. Dramatic beats
texto:
```text
0-5s    Hook.        Hero already in tension. No setup. Problem on screen.
5-15s   Context.     Where we are. Who is near. What is at stake.
15-30s  Pressure.    Hero tries to hold control.
30-45s  Crack.       A detail appears that breaks the hero's position.
45-60s  Acceleration. Cuts shorten. Breath tightens.
60-75s  Impact.      Decision, break, confession, or action.
75-90s  Aftermath.   Brief silence or visual residue.
```

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 1. Dramatic beats
texto: Adjust for 30s or 15s by compressing proportionally. Never skip the Crack or the Impact.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: ### Layer 2. Shot functions

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: Tag every shot with a function. Same taxonomy as in role-modes.md, expanded with Power.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Establish.** Where we are.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Power.** Who controls the scene right now.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Pressure.** What is pushing down on the hero.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Detail.** Object, hand, phone, eye, drop, receipt, door. Macro anchor.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Reaction.** Face after the event.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Shift.** Inner change made visible.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Impact.** The decisive frame.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Aftermath.** Emptiness after action.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: - **Exit.** Final image the viewer carries out.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 2. Shot functions
texto: This is cinema grammar. Everything else is decorative wallpaper.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: ### Layer 3. Editing rhythm

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: Not random mincing. A rhythmic staircase.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto:
```text
long - shorter - shorter - pause - impact
```

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: Example internal structure of an 8-10 second montage.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: - 4s. Wide. Hero enters.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: - 2s. Medium. Hero notices the object.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: - 1s. Close-up. Eyes.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: - 12 frames (0.5s). Macro insert of the object.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: - 8 frames (0.33s). Hand.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: - 6 frames (0.25s). Detail / sound cue.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: - 2s. Sudden silence.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: - 1s. Decision.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 10. Three-layer storyboard method › Layer 3. Editing rhythm
texto: Rule. The pause before the impact is more important than the speed of the cuts. Without a pause, speed becomes visual meat grinder.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: ## 11. Shot card template

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: For each shot in a storyboard, fill every field. Missing fields reveal missing direction.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Beat.** What changes in the story here.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Emotion.** Fear, shame, anger, guilt, resolve, relief, etc.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Frame.** wide / medium / close-up / macro insert

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Composition.** Center, edge, negative space, reflection, silhouette, foreground obstruction.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Camera.** Static, push-in, handheld, tracking, whip-pan.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Movement reason.** Why the camera moves here. Answer "what changed?"

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Action.** Exact physical event.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Eye trace.** Where the viewer's gaze should land in the first 0.3s.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Duration.** 0.5s, 1s, 3s.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Cut type.** match cut, smash cut, cut on action, J-cut, L-cut.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Sound.** Breath, bass hit, street noise, phone ring, silence.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Light / color.** Cold, contrast, flicker, shadow, specific palette.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: - **Production note.** Prop, location, actor direction.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 11. Shot card template
texto: If a shot card has empty fields, fill them or drop the shot.

texto: ## 12. Rhythm ladder

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 12. Rhythm ladder
texto: Drama rhythm is not uniform. It is stepped.

texto: ### Slow-burn drama

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 12. Rhythm ladder › Anxiety build

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: ## 13. One-anchor principle

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: For any short dramatic piece, commit to exactly five anchors. No more.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - One main emotion.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - One visual motif.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - One anchor object.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - One break.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - One final image.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: Example.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - Emotion. Guilt.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - Motif. The hero keeps being reflected in glass surfaces (window, phone screen, elevator door).

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - Anchor object. A phone with one unread message.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - Break. The hero deletes the message.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: - Final image. The hero's face stays reflected in the darkened phone screen.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 13. One-anchor principle
texto: This set can be storyboarded, prompted, and cut together into something that carries real weight. It beats stacking "cinematic, professional, high quality, masterpiece" forever.

texto: ## 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt
texto: Run this six-point check before returning the final prompt to the user.

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt
texto: 1. Is the scene formula complete? (desire + obstacle + geometry + gaze + rhythm)

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt
texto: 2. Does every shot pass the three-detail check? (environmental pressure + physical micro-action + sound or visual motif)

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt
texto: 3. Does every shot do one of the three jobs? (change emotion, advance action, increase pressure)

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt
texto: 4. Is there a motivated reason for every camera move?

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt
texto: 5. Is the spatial geometry readable?

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt
texto: 6. Are the five anchors named? (emotion, motif, object, break, final image)

encabezado: Dramaturgy, detail, montage › 15. Dramaturgy check before sending any prompt
texto: If any answer is no, fix before sending. Step 2 is the most violated.

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › One continuous take instead of montage
texto: ### One continuous take instead of montage

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › One continuous take instead of montage
texto: Fix.

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › One continuous take instead of montage
texto:
```text
This must be a multi-shot sequence with visible hard cuts. Do not generate a single continuous take. Each beat uses a different angle and framing.
```

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › One continuous take instead of montage
texto: For Seedance specifically, add explicit `Cut to.` or `Camera cut to.` markers in the prompt body.

texto: ### Character face changes between shots

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Character face changes between shots
texto: Fix.

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Character face changes between shots
texto:
```text
Preserve the exact character in every shot. Same face shape, same eye color, same hair, same clothing, same expression style. [repeat the full identity block]
```

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Character face changes between shots
texto: For Kling. Use Element Binding with 3-4 reference images (front, side, three-quarter).

```text
Track the object continuously. The same object remains visible or clearly implied in every beat.
```

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Object disappears mid-scene
texto: Describe the object's state progression in one sentence. "The sausage moves. fridge -> pot -> fork -> floor."

texto: ### Weak drama. Scene feels flat.

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Weak drama. Scene feels flat.
texto: Fix.

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Weak drama. Scene feels flat.
texto:
```text
Play the scene with full emotional seriousness. Treat the ordinary object as if it carries life-or-death meaning. No comedy pacing. No detached observation.
```


texto: Fix. Avoid style words like "hyperrealistic 8k masterpiece." These push the model into AI-art territory. Use production language instead.

texto: ### Twins / face-blending in multi-person scenes

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Twins / face-blending in multi-person scenes
texto: Two or more characters converge into near-identical faces, or background extras clone the hero.

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Twins / face-blending in multi-person scenes
texto: Fix. Bind each subject to its own reference individually (see `universal-rules.md` U13), then force differentiation.


encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 2. Common failures and fixes › Objects or characters appear too early in an extension

texto: For forward extensions, the standard clause: "prohibit rigid cutting, prohibit objects appearing out of thin air."

texto: ## 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons › Seedance
texto: ### Seedance

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons › Seedance
texto:
```text
Subject. [identity block].
Motion. [one clear present-tense action].
Camera. Shot 1. [framing, lens, movement]. Cut to. Shot 2. [framing, lens, movement]. Cut to. Shot 3. [framing, lens, movement].
Environment. [location, time, props].
Lighting. [source, direction, quality, color].
Style. [realism level, genre reference].
Audio. [ambient, SFX]. (1.5+ only)
Continuity. [what must remain constant].

--resolution 1080p --duration 5 --camerafixed false
```

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons › Kling text-to-video
texto: ### Kling text-to-video

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons › Kling text-to-video
texto:
```text
[Subject with identity anchor]. [Subject movement]. Scene. [3-5 environment elements]. Camera. [one movement + lens]. Lighting. [source + quality]. Atmosphere. [mood].

Negative field. blurry, distorted hands, extra fingers, melted face, watermark, subtitles, jitter.
```

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons › Kling image-to-video
texto: ### Kling image-to-video

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons › Kling image-to-video
texto:
```text
Preserve [silhouette / feature / label]. [Camera movement, one lens]. [One or two motion verbs]. [Atmospheric cue, light change].

Negative field. blurry, distorted hands, melted face, jitter.
```

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons › Veo prose
texto: ### Veo prose

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 3. Cross-model prompt skeletons › Veo prose
texto:
```text
[Subject performing action] in [environment]. [Camera framing + lens + movement]. [Lighting direction + color]. [Style + mood + palette].

Audio: [ambient, SFX, music texture].
Says: [character] says, "[dialogue, max 8s of speech]."
SFX: [punctual sound events].

Duration: [4 / 6 / 8] seconds.
```

texto: ## 4. Default negative constraints

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 4. Default negative constraints
texto: Where negatives are supported (Kling field, Veo body text, Seedance 2.0 fragile).

encabezado: Fixes, checklist, and cross-model skeletons › 4. Default negative constraints
texto:
```text
No subtitles. No on-screen text. No extra characters. No changing clothes. No changing face. No logos. No cartoon physics unless requested. No warm yellow tones unless requested. No random camera drift. No single-take when multi-shot is requested. No distorted hands. No extra fingers.
```

texto: For Seedance 1.0. Invert all negatives to positive phrasings in the prompt body.

texto: ## 1. What Kling is

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 1. What Kling is
texto: Strong at realistic physics, character animation, and consistency through reference images. Fast generation. Best for social-ready clips and repeat-character scenes.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 1. What Kling is
texto: **Kling 3.0** changed the model's positioning fundamentally — it now competes with Seedance on multi-shot output (up to 6 shots per generation) and with Veo on native dialogue and lip-sync. See section 3.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: ## 2. Versions and element limits

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: Kling models vary widely in how many distinct elements they can handle in a single prompt. Overstuffing produces melting faces, broken hands, or static motion.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: - **Kling 1.6.** Simplified prompts. Keep it very simple.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: - **Kling 2.1 Pro.** 1080p at 30fps. Motion Brush. End frame control.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: - **Kling 2.5 Turbo Pro.** Maximum 3-4 distinct elements.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: - **Kling 2.6 Pro.** 5-7 elements. Motion Control. Element Binding for character consistency.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: - **Kling 3.0.** Multi-shot in one generation (up to 6 shots). Native audio with dialogue and lip-sync. 15s continuous output. Native 4K, up to 60 fps. Strongest character and scene consistency. Two tiers: v3/pro and v3/standard.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: - **Kling 3.0 Turbo** (June 2026). Speed/price tier: audio included in base cost, noticeably better lip-sync on talking heads, 3-15s, but capped at 1080p — no 4K.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: - **Kling 3.0 Omni** (June 2026). The reference-and-editing flagship (API alias `o3`): strongest input understanding, editing pipeline at 3-15s with 4K in/out, Elements 3.0 with voice binding (see section 7).

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 2. Versions and element limits
texto: If in doubt about the user's version, ask. The prompting protocol differs between 1.x – 2.x (sections 4-9) and 3.0 (section 3).

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Anchor subjects early
texto: ### Anchor subjects early

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Anchor subjects early
texto: Introduce every character and key object at the **start** of the prompt, before any shot description. Use unique consistent identifiers — the same label survives across all shots:

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Anchor subjects early
texto:
```text
[Character A: Exhausted Partner — late 40s, gray-streaked beard, navy peacoat, hollow eyes]
[Character B: Female Investor — early 30s, sharp blazer, calm posture]
```

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Anchor subjects early
texto: Then refer to them as "Character A" / "Character B" inside shot descriptions. This locks identity better than re-describing the character each shot.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Multi-shot syntax (think in shots, not clips)
texto: ### Multi-shot syntax (think in shots, not clips)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Multi-shot syntax (think in shots, not clips)
texto:
```text
[Character A: ...]
[Character B: ...]

Master intent: tense negotiation in a glass-walled office at dusk.

Shot 1 (0-3s). Wide tracking shot. Character A enters frame from left, crosses to the table.
Shot 2 (3-6s). Profile close-up on Character A. He sets down a brown leather folder.
Shot 3 (6-9s). Shot-reverse-shot. Cut to Character B's face. She does not blink.
Shot 4 (9-12s). Macro insert on her hand tightening around a fountain pen.
Shot 5 (12-15s). Two-shot, low angle, both reflected in the glass wall behind them.

Camera. Slow, deliberate. Sony FX6 feel, 35mm and 85mm.
Lighting. Cold blue dusk through floor-to-ceiling windows. Single amber desk lamp.
Audio. Distant city ambience. No music. Footsteps on hardwood. Pen clicks on paper.
```

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Multi-shot syntax (think in shots, not clips)
texto: Each shot must answer: **framing + subject + motion**. Empty shot descriptions ("static frame, ambient mood") collapse into one continuous take.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: ### Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: For any speaking scene, follow these four rules. The fal.ai guide calls them P1, P2, P3, P4.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: **P1. Structured naming.** Use unique identifiers per character.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: - ✓ `[Character A: Black-suited Agent]` and `[Character B: Female Assistant]`

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: - ✗ "[Agent] says... Then, he says..."

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: **P2. Visual anchoring before dialogue.** Bind dialogue to a unique action first.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: - ✓ "Character A pulls a folded note from his pocket and reads aloud: 'It's not what you think.'"

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: - ✗ "Character A says 'It's not what you think.'" (no visual anchor → lip-sync drifts)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: **P3. Voice tone in the tag.** Assign emotion / texture inline.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: - ✓ `[Character A, raspy deep voice]: "We're out of time."`

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: - ✓ `[Character B, clear fearful voice]: "Don't open it."`

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: - ✗ `[Man]: "We're out of time."` (vague — model picks a generic voice)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Dialogue protocol (P1-P4)
texto: **P4. Temporal control between lines.** Use linking words to prevent dialogue from merging.

texto: ### Image-to-video on 3.0 — lock first, then move

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Image-to-video on 3.0 — lock first, then move
texto: The input image serves as the anchor for identity, layout, and on-image text. Keep the prompt short and motion-focused. Describe **how the scene evolves from the image**, not what is in the image.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Image-to-video on 3.0 — lock first, then move
texto:
```text
Preserve identity, wardrobe, and the storefront sign exactly.
[Character A: same person from the image]
Shot 1 (0-2s). She turns her head toward camera, exhales.
Shot 2 (2-5s). Slow push-in to a tight close-up. Wind catches her hair.
Audio. Distant traffic, wind through awnings, a soft bell from inside the shop.
```

texto: ### Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands
texto: Use these terms directly — the model treats them as instructions, not flavor:

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands
texto: - Framing: profile shot, three-quarter, macro insert, two-shot, OTS, POV, low angle, high angle, Dutch

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands
texto: - Edits: shot-reverse-shot, match cut, smash cut, J-cut, L-cut

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands
texto: - Camera moves: tracking, dolly, push-in, pull-out, whip pan, crane, handheld, orbital / 360 spin, Steadicam, drone-like aerial. Composites work: "pan right while tilting up".

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands
texto: - Lens feel: 35mm, 50mm, 85mm, 100mm macro, anamorphic 40mm

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands
texto: - Tempo words the model obeys: "ultra-slow motion" (2-3s feel), "slow and deliberate" (5-8s), "moderate" (3-5s), "quick snap" (1-2s); exact timing works too ("5-second dolly zoom").

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands
texto: - Angle carries emotion: low angle = dominance, high angle = vulnerability, eye-level = neutral. Pick per the power dynamic from `dramaturgy.md` §6, not at random.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Cinematic vocabulary that 3.0 actually understands
texto: - In the Kling app, Master Shot presets ("Move Forward and Zoom Up" etc.) are more stable than hand-written camera prose and save credits — prefer them for standard moves, prose for motivated ones.

texto: Within the 3.0 family: talking heads and dialogue on a budget → **Turbo** (best lip-sync per dollar, audio included, 1080p cap); reference-heavy or editing work, 4K delivery → **Omni**; everything else → base 3.0.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 3. Kling 3.0 — multi-shot, native audio, 15s › Default model choice
texto: For everything else (single clip, no dialogue, < 10s, character lock via reference images, Motion Brush) — older versions still work and are cheaper.

texto: ## 6. Negative prompts (critical rule)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 6. Negative prompts (critical rule)
texto: Kling has a dedicated negative prompts field. The field auto-interprets input as exclusion. Do not write "no X". Write the thing itself.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 6. Negative prompts (critical rule)

Bad. "no robots"
Good. "robots"

Bad. "no blurry faces, no distorted hands"
Good. "blurry faces, distorted hands, melted features"

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 6. Negative prompts (critical rule)
texto: Common effective negatives.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 6. Negative prompts (critical rule)

```text
low resolution, blurry, distorted hands, extra fingers, melted face, watermark, subtitles, logo, text overlay, jitter, shaking camera, deformed
```

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 6. Negative prompts (critical rule)

texto: For character consistency across generations, Kling has an Element Library. Upload 3-4 reference images of the character from different angles.

texto: Then in Image-to-Video settings, enable "Bind Elements" to lock features. This gives the AI a visual anchor that survives camera pans and light changes.

texto: Source image rules.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x)
texto: - 1080p or higher.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x)
texto: - Even lighting. Avoid hard shadows. The AI can mistake them for permanent facial features.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x)
texto: - No text or watermarks.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x)
texto: - Clean uncluttered background.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x)
texto: For Kling 3.0 — Element Library still works, but the in-prompt `[Character A: ...]` labels (see section 3) are usually enough on their own.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x) › Elements 3.0 (Omni)
texto: ### Elements 3.0 (Omni)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x) › Elements 3.0 (Omni)
texto: On 3.0 Omni the element system got deeper:

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x) › Elements 3.0 (Omni)
texto: - A character element takes either a **3-8s video** (the model extracts both appearance and voice) or up to **4 multi-angle stills** (front, three-quarter, profile, back), plus optional **voice binding** (5-30s audio clip). Once bound, the voice belongs to the subject — do not re-describe it in the prompt.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x) › Elements 3.0 (Omni)
texto: - Define a character / product / location **once** as an element, then tag it in prose: `@Grace picks up the folder`. The prompt carries only action and camera; identity lives in the element.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x) › Elements 3.0 (Omni)
texto: - Holds 3+ distinct characters in frame without feature blending — but only if **each** has its own element.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 7. Element Library and Element Binding (1.x – 2.x) › Elements 3.0 (Omni)
texto: - Cost of the feature: several practitioners report visible image-quality degradation the moment elements/references are enabled. Use elements only when consistency actually matters; for one-off clips, in-prompt labels are cleaner.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 8. Motion Brush (unique)
texto: ## 8. Motion Brush (unique)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 8. Motion Brush (unique)
texto: Animate up to 6 regions of a single image independently. Each region gets its own motion path.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 8. Motion Brush (unique)
texto: Critical rule. The text prompt MUST match the brush motion. If you brush a river flowing and write "stagnant pond" the model tears itself apart. Align prompt verbs with brush directions.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 9. Motion Control (2.6 Pro, unique)
texto: ## 9. Motion Control (2.6 Pro, unique)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 9. Motion Control (2.6 Pro, unique)
texto: Copy motion from a reference video. Use when you need specific performance or choreography (dance, martial arts, specific gait). The prompt then focuses on subject description only, the reference handles motion.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 10. Image-to-video rule
texto: ## 10. Image-to-video rule

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 10. Image-to-video rule
texto: Keep the prompt short (20-40 words). Focus only on motion. Do not re-describe static elements the model already sees.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 10. Image-to-video rule
texto: Include explicit continuity cues. Kling responds well to "preserve X" instructions.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 10. Image-to-video rule
texto: Example.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 10. Image-to-video rule
texto:
```text
Preserve silhouette and label text. Slow tracking shot from the side. She turns her head toward camera. Wind catches her hair. 35mm, golden hour rim light.
```

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 10. Image-to-video rule
texto: For Kling 3.0 image-to-video — see section 3 ("Image-to-video on 3.0 — lock first, then move").

texto: ## 11. Failure modes and fixes

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Random camera drift in static scenes
texto: ### Random camera drift in static scenes

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Random camera drift in static scenes
texto: Fix. Say "locked static frame" or "camera fixed, no movement."

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Prompt exceeds model capacity, output melts
texto: ### Prompt exceeds model capacity, output melts

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Prompt exceeds model capacity, output melts
texto: Fix. Cut to model-appropriate element count. 3-4 for Turbo, 5-7 for 2.6 Pro.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Character face changes between generations
texto: ### Character face changes between generations

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Character face changes between generations
texto: Fix. Upload 3-4 reference images to Element Library. Use Bind Elements in the settings.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Negative prompts ignored
texto: ### Negative prompts ignored

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Negative prompts ignored
texto: Fix. Rewrite "no X" as "X" in the negative field.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Motion Brush artifact
texto: ### Motion Brush artifact

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Motion Brush artifact
texto: Fix. Check that the text prompt verbs match the brush direction. Rewrite the text if it contradicts the motion.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Element overload melts hands
texto: ### Element overload melts hands

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Element overload melts hands
texto: Fix. Simplify. Combine elements where possible. Cut secondary descriptions.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Kling 3.0 collapses multi-shot into one continuous take
texto: ### Kling 3.0 collapses multi-shot into one continuous take

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Kling 3.0 collapses multi-shot into one continuous take
texto: Fix. Make shot boundaries explicit: `Shot 1 (0-3s). ... Shot 2 (3-6s). ...`. Each shot description must include a different framing or camera angle. If two adjacent shots share both framing and angle, the model merges them.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Kling 3.0 dialogue lip-sync drifts
texto: ### Kling 3.0 dialogue lip-sync drifts

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Kling 3.0 dialogue lip-sync drifts
texto: Fix. Apply P2 — bind dialogue to a unique visual action ("Character A pulls a folded note from his pocket and reads aloud:") before the line itself. Then add P4 linking words ("Immediately,") between consecutive lines.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Kling 3.0 picks the wrong voice
texto: ### Kling 3.0 picks the wrong voice

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Kling 3.0 picks the wrong voice
texto: Fix. Apply P3 — put voice tone inside the speaker tag: `[Character A, raspy deep voice]:`. Generic `[Man]:` / `[Woman]:` tags get a generic voice.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Image quality drops when Elements / references are enabled
texto: ### Image quality drops when Elements / references are enabled

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Image quality drops when Elements / references are enabled
texto: Fix. Strip references to the essential ones only; for one-off clips prefer in-prompt `[Character A: ...]` labels over elements. Accept the trade: elements buy consistency, not fidelity.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Two similar characters blend features in one frame
texto: ### Two similar characters blend features in one frame

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Two similar characters blend features in one frame
texto: Fix. Give each character its own element (or its own labeled identity block). Never let two speaking characters share one visual description.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Morphing artifacts on fast motion
texto: ### Morphing artifacts on fast motion

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Morphing artifacts on fast motion
texto: Fix. Generate the action in slow motion and speed it up in post — the model holds geometry at slower internal motion.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Music appears even though the prompt says "no music"
texto: ### Music appears even though the prompt says "no music"

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 11. Failure modes and fixes › Music appears even though the prompt says "no music"
texto: Fix. Negative-prompting music is unreliable. Generate with `generate_audio` off and add sound in post, or strip the music track.

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 12. Skeleton › Multi-shot with dialogue (Kling 3.0)
texto: ### Multi-shot with dialogue (Kling 3.0)

encabezado: Kling reference (Kuaishou) › 12. Skeleton › Multi-shot with dialogue (Kling 3.0)
texto:
```text
[Character A: Investigator — late 30s, navy raincoat, tired blue eyes, three-day stubble]
[Character B: Witness — early 20s, oversized hoodie, hands wrapped around a paper cup, eyes red from crying]

Master intent: a 12-second interrogation in a fluorescent-lit precinct break room at 2am. The investigator holds back, the witness breaks.

Shot 1 (0-3s). Two-shot, eye level, 35mm. Character A sits across from Character B. Static frame.
Shot 2 (3-6s). OTS over Character A's shoulder. Character B's hands tighten on the paper cup.
Shot 3 (6-9s). Profile close-up on Character A. He slides a photo across the table.
[Character A, low even voice]: "You were there."
Shot 4 (9-12s). Reverse — close-up on Character B. She does not look up.
Immediately, [Character B, fragile broken voice]: "I didn't see anything."

Camera. Locked frames, no movement except the slide of the photo. Sony FX6 feel.
Lighting. Cold overhead fluorescent, slight flicker. Pale skin, hard shadows under the eyes.
Audio. Distant police radio chatter, the buzz of the fluorescent tube, a vending machine humming in the corridor. No music.

Negative field. blurry, distorted hands, extra fingers, melted face, watermark, subtitles, jitter, dialogue overlap.
```

texto: # Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage
texto: Domain grammar for dynamic race spots — drag, drift, chase, drag-strip, kinetic montage. The brief is brutal: faces are banned, the deliverable is **still keyframes (opornye kadry)** for an animatic, and a frozen panel must read as lethal velocity at a glance. Speed is not a post effect — it is a photographic fact built from spatial cues that imply the missing motion. Emotion does not live on a face; it rides on metal, rubber, road, gauges and light. Load this file when the task involves racing, drift, drag, chase, speed, dynamic or kinetic montage, "гонщик", or "раскадровка гонки".

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage
texto: This file **specializes `animatic-keyframes.md` for the race domain.** That file owns the general still-panel method and is the prerequisite read: the keyframe card, the **six motion-as-still cues** (§4), the **5-cue speed budget** (§4), the **EMOTION→OBJECT substitution table** and state-change cheat-sheet (§5), the loaded-frame depth method (§6), the **density ladder** (§3), the **keyframe→image-gen prompt skeleton** (§7), the worked 30s board (§8), and the **master per-panel checklist** (§9). This file does **not** repeat them — it adds the race grammar on top: the schools, the start-line liturgy, the shot families, the drift ritual, the Christmas-Tree light logic, and the cold-combat palette. Where the method is general, this file points; where it is race-specific, it teaches.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage
texto: Sits on top of `dramaturgy.md` (§2 Details Law, §3 fantik, §9 environment, §11 shot card, §12 rhythm ladder, §15 check), `universal-rules.md` (U1–U12), `role-modes.md` §4 (shot-function taxonomy). Pairs with `camera-lighting-vocabulary.md` for framing/lens/light tokens, `patterns-and-genres.md` for the action/escalation arc, and `seedance.md` / `kling.md` / `veo.md` to animate each locked keyframe.

Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)
texto: ## 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)
texto: Six laws govern every race panel. Break one and the spot collapses to a car commercial.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)
texto: 1. **Authentic speed, never CGI-clean or sped-up.** Build velocity into the static composition (§3); never lean on a ramp to rescue a dead frame. Over-crank, glass-smooth stabilization and post speed-ramps read subconsciously as "ad-speed" and drain all threat. Squat, lifted nose, slick wrinkle, smeared rim — the physics has to be visible in the still.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)
texto: 2. **Detail is the emotion.** Faces banned, feeling renders only on a knuckle, a needle, a pedal, smoke, or a sweat bead (`dramaturgy.md` §2; the full substitution method is `animatic-keyframes.md` §5). A hand mid-grip is the no-face equivalent of a close-up on the eyes. No abstract "motion", no named feeling.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)
texto: 3. **One governing visual promise per piece.** A 30s cut earns cohesion from a single conceit: everything through reflections in painted metal, or everything through circles (tach → headlight → bulb → wheel), or everything as machine-talks / no-music. Kon's "one visual principle". Name it before boarding.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)
texto: 4. **Beat-locked cutting.** Loudness in the audio = shot count on the board (§8; the density ladder itself is `animatic-keyframes.md` §3). Silence = one held panel. Bang = a burst of 4–8-frame micro-panels. Cut length is engine RPM made visual: idle = long panels, redline = collapsing panels toward the green.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)
texto: 5. **Cold combative palette** (§7). Steel blue, cyan, magenta, dirty mercury-white; **red as danger accent only** (brake glow, redline, tail-lights, the Tree's bulbs). No warm cozy amber wash — warmth appears only as toxin. Steal Tony Scott's grain, contrast and overexposure; **discard his warm grade.**

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 1. Core laws (the non-negotiables)
texto: 6. **Every insert is load-bearing.** Each detail panel must be captionable with one race label — *setup / commitment / mistake / recovery / proof-of-speed / result* (§4). If you cannot label it, it is a *fantik* (`dramaturgy.md` §3) — drop it. A board that is all proof-of-speed with no commitment/mistake/recovery is a reel, not a story.

Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 2. Four schools worth stealing
texto: ## 2. Four schools worth stealing

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 2. Four schools worth stealing
texto: Four traditions, compressed. Each ends in its one transferable rule.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 2. Four schools worth stealing
texto:
**Kinetic montage (Wright, Ritchie, Boyle, Scott, Vaughn, Raimi, Aronofsky).** Time is elastic, every prop is a trigger, prep is an event. A keyframe cannot ramp or whip — so each moving trick compresses into one frozen cue (the six cues are catalogued in `animatic-keyframes.md` §4). Aronofsky's hip-hop montage is the single most transferable engine for prep-without-faces: a 6–9-panel ultra-CU strip of the start ritual, each panel one beat with a locked sound cue, the cluster **repeated two-to-three times with escalation** (calm → strained → violent). Repetition is memory; memory is emotion.
→ **Rule:** never write "motion" — write the artifact motion leaves behind, and never board a neutral panel (every frame carries a forward vector, negative space ahead of the subject).

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 2. Four schools worth stealing
texto:
**Race-truth (Frankenheimer, Lelouch, Mangold/Papamichael, Howard/Dod Mantle, Refn).** Speed is a fact you earn by putting the camera where a real rig could bolt — bumper, hood lip, hostess-tray, axle, cabin. Low, wide and close, hard-mounted without vibration isolation so "cheeks shake", asphalt streaking in frame as the speedometer, mini-cams next to pistons and swelling tires for "an electron-microscope view of the car at its limit". Refn's cocoon: silence and stillness inside the shell, chaos outside, so the launch detonates. Refuse the crank — *Grand Prix* oiled tires for real smoke rather than fake the burnout.
→ **Rule:** if the implied camera could not physically mount on the car, the panel reads as render — drop it to bumper height and bolt it on.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 2. Four schools worth stealing
texto:
**Loaded composition (Bong, Park, Anderson, Kon).** With no faces, geometry and the depth stack do the acting (the FG/MG/BG depth method is `animatic-keyframes.md` §6). One geometric spine (centerline or Christmas Tree as the axis); every object an evidence (Park: "each object is a clue") or it is cut. Symmetry is handwriting — one held symmetric "breath" frame says balanced rivalry; break it the instant one car noses ahead. Kon's graphic-match pairs compress time across two adjacent keyframes sharing a shape at the same size and screen position.
→ **Rule:** a panel answers one question in the first glance and rewards a second look — one focal point, one emotion, three depth layers, zero dead objects.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 2. Four schools worth stealing
texto:
**Rule-based ad (Honda *Cog*, Audi Quattro, Nike/Ritchie, Goodyear).** The drama is pure mechanism: every object does something irreversible, "let the machine talk" (no music), the entire spot first-person with no hero face. Tension is "will it fire". A static fetish shot of a gear lever flatlines; an object crossing a threshold says a decision just happened.
→ **Rule:** objects carry feeling only when they visibly **change state** — board the "after" (needle pinned in the red, ignition lamp blooming live, slick caught mid-fold), the "before" is implied.

Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 3. Selling speed in a single frame
texto: ## 3. Selling speed in a single frame

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 3. Selling speed in a single frame
texto: A still has no engine note and zero motion. It sells velocity through the **speed-budget rule** — a frame reads fast only when **≥3 of five cues coexist** (camera at/below bumper height · asphalt streaking the lower frame · a near foreground reference passing the edge · sharp hero against motion-blurred background · a mechanical-vibration cue). The full rule, with the anti-fake firewall, lives in `animatic-keyframes.md` §4; do not re-derive it. One cue is a car photo; three is velocity; five and even a parked car reads dangerous. If a "fast" panel can't name three, reframe lower, drag the camera to the asphalt, throw a barrier into the foreground.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 3. Selling speed in a single frame

texto: ## 4. Storytelling without faces — the race captioning system

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 4. Storytelling without faces — the race captioning system
texto: A face does four jobs: internal state, where it looks, the cost, the decision. Banned, those jobs redistribute — **decision → anatomy mid-action; internal state → an object crossing a threshold; looking/rivalry → space.** The mechanism, the EMOTION→OBJECT substitution table and the state-change cheat-sheet are owned by `animatic-keyframes.md` §5; do not duplicate them. Two filters before you draw: name the **verb** on any hand/foot panel (grip / latch / shift / preload / release — no verb, no panel), and board only the **after** state of any object threshold (Honda *Cog*). Pick ONE hero object and board it three times at rising intensity — beats twelve unrelated inserts (`dramaturgy.md` §13).

texto: What this file owns is the **race captioning system** — the margin label that proves an insert is load-bearing (Law 6). Every detail keyframe gets exactly one. If you cannot assign one, drop the panel.

texto: ## 5. The race ritual (liturgy) + the 5 shot families

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 5. The race ritual (liturgy) + the 5 shot families
texto: The race is not a chase, it is a *liturgy*. Every phase is a legible, irreversible state-change a knowing viewer reads instantly — muddle the order and the spot dies. The countdown *tightens cut length toward the green*, then explodes: the drag-specific instance of the `dramaturgy.md` §12 rhythm staircase. Draw one anchor keyframe per beat. In a faceless spot **Reaction** is reassigned from a human face to the *machine's* face — the needle jumping, the slick wrinkling, the nose squatting. Gauges and rubber are the actor.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 5. The race ritual (liturgy) + the 5 shot families
texto: **Amber logic (decision point).** Choose the **Sportsman / full tree** for an ad: three ambers fire *sequentially 0.5s apart* — three drawable keyframes, a stretched drum-roll of dread with cut length collapsing toward the green. The Pro tree fires all three at once — one panel, brutal but no build. Draw the Sportsman stagger. Always leave on the **last amber, not the green** (holeshot): the launch keyframe precedes the green-lit panel by a frame, which makes it read as *anticipation*, not reaction.

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 5. The race ritual (liturgy) + the 5 shot families
texto: **Drift adaptation — the slip-angle liturgy.** Drift swaps the countdown for a *continuous angle ritual*: **approach → entry → clutch-kick initiation → counter-steer hold → clipping point (wall proximity) → smoke wall → transition (flick) → exit.** The **counter-steer** replaces the slick-wrinkle as the "physics made visible" anchor — ECU/CU of hands wound into opposite lock, forearms crossed, wheel at full angle, cold side-light on knuckles, the steering angle drawn large and unmistakable. **Wall proximity** is danger without a face: barrier hard and sharp in the foreground layer, car door a hand's-width away, motion-streak on the wall texture — the gap *is* the emotion. The **transition flick** is yawed mid-switch, smoke crossing the frame diagonally, both exit directions readable.

Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 7. Light & color for speed without faces
texto: ## 7. Light & color for speed without faces

encabezado: Race, speed and faceless kinetic montage › 7. Light & color for speed without faces
texto: Faces are banned, so light is the only actor left. It does not "set a mood" — it **rims a material** so a piece of metal, rubber or skin reports the emotion a face would. General light grammar (sources, direction, quality) is `camera-lighting-vocabulary.md` §4–7; the anti-sterile firewall is `animatic-keyframes.md` §7 + `universal-rules.md` U12. The race-specific governing law: *embrace the dark* (crush blacks, ~70% of the frame unlit), *one motivated practical per panel* (Tree lamp, headlight, sodium lamp, brake glow), *light is specular not ambient* (every panel needs ≥1 hard specular hit — no specular, no information).
